newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Interest rate bogey weighs on Euro bourses.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Interest rate bogey weighs on Euro bourses.

text.p: Leading European shares were lower on Tuesday, nervously awaiting the start of trade on Wall Street, and dealers said market sentiment was weighed on by continuing interest rate worries.

Blue chips in London, Frankfurt and Paris were all down despite another record close on Wall Street overnight. Dealers said worries about possible U.S. rate hikes and near-term British credit tightening plus fears the Dow could be hit by profit-taking were all taking their toll.

On the currency markets, the dollar was steady at the European mid-session in thin business and dealers said underlying bullish sentiment was intact, though the U.S. currency slipped overnight from 45-month highs against the yen after Japanese officials again warned against excessive yen weakness.

In London, Europe's busiest stock exchange, shares started mixed and fell lower as sentiment suffered from a scarcity of corporate news and concerns about high interest rates -- which would make equities relatively less attractive to investors.
"People are expecting (UK) rates to go up sometime this quarter but until the rate picture becomes clear the uncertainty will remain and dog the market," one dealer commented.
The course of trading in New York was also a worry: "It's been another disappointing morning. Nobody wants to do anything until they see how Wall Street opens," one senior dealer said.
Analysts still expect the London share market to test its all-time highs in coming weeks but the spectre of higher interest rates should limit the upside.

"The FTSE's uptrend is still intact and it could test new highs in the near-term," said Kirit Shah, strategist at Sanwa International. "But with the bond market already factoring in a U.S. rate hike, the market will remain volatile."

In Frankfurt, German shares were down in pre-bourse electronic trade and also slightly weaker in morning bourse trade, unmoved by news of German industrial orders rising an expected 0.5 percent in November compared to October.
Other factors damping the market were a steep decline in Japanese stocks overnight and slightly softer German government bonds, dealers said.

In Paris French shares managed to cut some of their losses after opening lower on weaker bond prices and caution ahead of key U.S. statistics due out later in the week -- Thursday's producer price index and Friday's non-farm payrolls -- which will give clues to future movements of U.S. interest rates.

In currencies, the yen's partial recovery came after comments from finance minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, who said: "An excessively weak or strong yen is not favourable for the Japanese economy. We want exchange rates to stabilise."
Analysts regarded the comments as pre-emptive strikes against a quickly falling yen but they said it was unlikely Tokyo would take action to strengthen the currency.
The comeback by the yen did little to boost Tokyo stocks and the Nikkei average fell a sharp 2.83 percent to its lowest close in more than a year on deepening jitters about Japan's economy.

The dollar also slipped against the mark after Bundesbank president Tietmeyer was quoted as saying he saw no need for German interest rate policy to change for the time being. The dollar was holding above 1.5600 marks but was weaker than the 1.5665 marks seen late in Europe on Monday.
The only data of note due on Tuesday were U.S. factory goods orders for November due at 1300 GMT, which are forecast to show around a 0.6 percent decline compared with a 0.9 percent rise in October.
CURRENCIES AT 1145 GMT
The dollar was quoted around 1.5615 marks and 115.50 yen compared with 1.5665 marks and 115.60 yen in late European trade on Monday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1145 GMT
The FTSE 100 index of key British shares was 19.9 points lower at 4,086.6. The 30-share DAX index in Frankfurt was 1.48 points down at 2,879.84 In Paris, the CAC-40 index was down 3.11 at 2,303.51.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold fixed at $357.65, down slightly from London's Monday close of $357.95. Silver was up one cent at $4.68.
